title: Forms of Market
description: Class 11 / ISC Economics: the forms of market — perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly — their features and a side-by-side comparison.

topics.title: Monopoly
topics.concept:
We have seen perfect competition — many sellers of an identical product, all price takers. Real markets, however, range from many sellers to a single seller. The main forms of market are: perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly. The opposite extreme to perfect competition is monopoly.

A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes. The word comes from "mono" (one) and "poly" (seller). Its main features:

  • One seller, many buyers — the single firm is the whole industry.
  • No close substitutes for the product.
  • Strong barriers to entry — other firms cannot enter (due to law, patents, control of a raw material, or huge size).
  • The firm is a price maker — unlike a competitive firm, a monopolist can set the price (though it still faces the demand curve, so it must choose a price–quantity combination).

Because the monopolist faces the whole market demand, its demand (AR) curve slopes downward, and its MR curve lies below AR (as we saw in the revenue chapter). Examples include the Indian Railways (historically) and a local electricity or water supplier. A monopoly can charge a higher price and earn larger profits than a competitive firm, which is why monopolies are often regulated by the government to protect consumers.

examples.solution:
One seller, no substitutes.

  • A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes.
examples.answer: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is a monopolist called a 'price maker'?
examples.solution:
It controls supply of the product.

  • As the only seller, it can set the price (choosing a price–quantity point on the demand curve).
examples.answer: Because as the sole seller it can set the price of the product (it is not forced to accept a market price).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does a monopoly face strong barriers to entry?
examples.solution:
Entry is blocked.

  • Due to law, patents, control of a key raw material, or very large size, other firms cannot enter.
examples.answer: Because legal restrictions, patents, control of a key input or huge size block other firms from entering.

recap:
• Forms of market: perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly.
  • Monopoly: single seller, no close substitutes, strong barriers to entry, firm is a price maker.
  • AR (demand) slopes downward, MR below AR; can charge higher price → often regulated.

options: A single seller with no close substitutes
quiz.explanation: A monopoly is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes.
As the only seller, a monopolist can set the price — a price maker.

topics.title: Monopolistic Competition
topics.concept:
Most real-world markets lie between the two extremes of perfect competition and monopoly. The most common is monopolistic competition — a market with many sellers selling similar but slightly different (differentiated) products. It combines elements of both competition (many firms) and monopoly (each firm has a unique brand). Its main features:

  • Many sellers and buyers — but not as many as in perfect competition.
  • Product differentiation — each firm's product is slightly different in brand, quality, packaging or design (e.g. different brands of toothpaste, soap, biscuits). This is the key feature.
  • Freedom of entry and exit.
  • Selling costs (advertising) — firms spend heavily on advertising to make their brand stand out.
  • Each firm has some control over its own price (because of its differentiated brand), so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve — but the control is limited because close substitutes are available from rivals.

Everyday markets like toothpaste, soap, restaurants, clothing and biscuits are good examples of monopolistic competition. The benefit to consumers is variety and choice; the drawback is the high cost of advertising and the slightly higher prices that brand differentiation allows. This is the market form closest to what we actually see around us.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the key feature of monopolistic competition?
examples.solution:
Products differ by brand.

  • Product differentiation — many firms sell similar but slightly different (branded) products.
examples.answer: Product differentiation — many firms selling similar but slightly different (branded) products.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give two real examples of monopolistic competition.
examples.solution:
Branded everyday goods.

  • Toothpaste brands and soap brands (also biscuits, restaurants, clothing).
examples.answer: Different brands of toothpaste and soap (also biscuits, restaurants, clothing).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why do firms in monopolistic competition spend heavily on advertising?
examples.solution:
To stand out from rivals.

  • To make their differentiated brand stand out and attract buyers.
examples.answer: To make their differentiated brand stand out from close substitutes and attract more buyers (selling costs).

recap:
• Monopolistic competition: many sellers, differentiated (branded) products, free entry/exit, heavy advertising.
  • Each firm has some price control (downward demand curve) but limited by close substitutes.
  • Examples: toothpaste, soap, restaurants. Benefit = variety/choice; drawback = ad costs.

quiz.q: The key feature of monopolistic competition is:

quiz.explanation: Many sellers with differentiated brands = monopolistic competition.

topics.title: Oligopoly and a Comparison of Market Forms
topics.concept:
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers ("oligo" means few). A special case with just two firms is a duopoly. Its main features:

  • A few large firms control most of the market.
  • Interdependence — this is the key feature. Because there are only a few firms, each one's actions (on price or output) strongly affect the others, so every firm must watch and react to its rivals' moves.
  • Strong barriers to entry (large size, high capital needs).
  • The product may be identical (e.g. steel, cement) or differentiated (e.g. cars).
  • Firms often avoid price wars and may instead collude or follow a price leader; non-price competition (advertising, features) is common.

Examples include the markets for cars, mobile phones, airlines, cement and telecom in India — each dominated by a handful of big companies. The table below compares the four forms of market:

FeaturePerfect comp.MonopolyMonopolisticOligopoly
No. of sellersVery manyOneManyFew
ProductIdenticalUniqueDifferentiatedSame or diff.
EntryFreeBlockedFreeDifficult
Price controlNone (taker)Full (maker)SomeSome (interdependent)

examples.problem: Example 1: What is an oligopoly, and what is its key feature?
examples.solution:
Few firms, watching each other.

  • A market dominated by a few large sellers.
  • Key feature: interdependence — each firm reacts to rivals' actions.
examples.answer: An oligopoly is a market with a few large sellers; its key feature is interdependence — each firm must react to its rivals' decisions.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give two real examples of oligopoly.
examples.solution:
Few-firm industries.

  • The car market and the telecom (mobile) market (also airlines, cement).
examples.answer: The car and telecom markets (also airlines and cement).

examples.problem: Example 3: Under which market form is the product identical and entry free?
examples.solution:
Use the comparison table.

  • Identical product + free entry + many sellers = perfect competition.
examples.answer: Perfect competition (very many sellers, identical product, free entry, price takers).

recap:
• Oligopoly: few large firms, key feature interdependence, barriers to entry, avoid price wars (collusion/price leader). (cars, telecom)
  • Compare: sellers (very many / one / many / few), product (identical / unique / differentiated / same-or-diff.), entry (free / blocked / free / difficult), price control (none / full / some / some).

quiz.q: An oligopoly is a market dominated by:
quiz.explanation: An oligopoly has a few large sellers.

quiz.q: The key feature of an oligopoly is:
quiz.explanation: With few firms, each reacts to rivals — interdependence.

questions.q: A market with a single seller and no close substitutes is a:
questions.explanation: A single seller with no close substitutes is a monopoly.

questions.q: The word 'monopoly' literally means:
questions.explanation: Mono = one, poly = seller — a single seller.

questions.q: A monopolist is a:
questions.explanation: As the sole seller, a monopolist can set the price.

questions.q: A feature of monopoly is:
questions.explanation: Monopoly has strong barriers preventing entry.

questions.q: A market with many sellers of differentiated products is:
questions.explanation: Many sellers + differentiated products = monopolistic competition.

questions.q: The key feature of monopolistic competition is:
questions.explanation: Product differentiation is its defining feature.

questions.q: Different brands of soap illustrate:
questions.explanation: Branded soaps with many sellers = monopolistic competition.

questions.q: Firms in monopolistic competition spend heavily on:
questions.explanation: They advertise to differentiate their brands.

questions.q: A market dominated by a few large sellers is an:
questions.explanation: A few large sellers form an oligopoly.

questions.q: An oligopoly with only two firms is a:
questions.explanation: Two firms make a duopoly (a special oligopoly).

questions.q: The key feature of oligopoly is:
questions.explanation: Few firms means each reacts to the others — interdependence.

questions.q: The car and telecom markets are examples of:
questions.explanation: A few big firms dominate these — oligopoly.

questions.q: Under perfect competition, entry of firms is:
questions.explanation: Perfect competition has free entry and exit.

questions.q: Under which market form does the firm have full control over price?
questions.explanation: A monopolist (single seller) has the most price control.

questions.q: The market form closest to what we see in everyday branded goods is:
questions.explanation: Everyday branded goods reflect monopolistic competition.

questions.q: A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, unlike a competitive firm, because the monopolist:
options: Is the whole market, so to sell more it must lower the price
questions.explanation: Being the entire industry, a monopolist's sales follow the market demand curve, which slopes down.

questions.q: Two toothpaste brands compete largely through advertising and packaging rather than big price cuts. This reflects:
questions.explanation: Differentiated-product firms rely on branding and advertising — non-price competition.

questions.q: When one airline in a four-firm market cuts fares, the others quickly match it. This behaviour shows the oligopoly feature of:
questions.explanation: Few firms watch and react to each other's moves — the essence of interdependence.

questions.q: A patent that prevents any other firm from making a drug for years helps create a:
questions.explanation: A patent is a legal barrier to entry, leaving a single seller — a monopoly.

questions.q: Compared with perfect competition, prices under monopolistic competition tend to be slightly higher mainly because of:
questions.explanation: Branding gives each firm some price power and adds selling costs, nudging prices above the competitive level.

questions.q: Which market form gives consumers the greatest variety of choice?
questions.explanation: Many differentiated brands offer the widest variety to consumers.

questions.q: Steel produced by a few large firms selling a near-identical product is an example of:
questions.explanation: Few firms selling a homogeneous product is an oligopoly (homogeneous oligopoly).

questions.q: Why are monopolies often regulated by the government?
options: To stop them charging excessive prices and protect consumers
questions.explanation: Without competition a monopolist can overcharge, so regulation protects consumers.

questions.q: Oligopoly firms often avoid aggressive price wars because a price cut by one is likely to:
options: Be matched by rivals, hurting everyone's profits
questions.explanation: Mutual matching of price cuts can leave all firms worse off, so they avoid price wars.

questions.q: Reading the comparison table, the form with 'one seller, unique product, blocked entry, full price control' is:
questions.explanation: Those four characteristics together describe a monopoly.
